title: Direct-object pronouns
subtitle: Refer without repeating
objectives: Identify direct objects in familiar sentences.
Choose and place lo, la, los and las.
Clarify a pronoun’s referent in a transaction.
warmup: Retrieve two sentences and one repair strategy from c2-u02. Change the subject or situation in each sentence and explain what changed. Then read today’s objectives and predict where your existing language may be insufficient.

lectures.title: Find what the verb affects
lectures.body: A direct object completes the action without an intervening recipient: Compro el libro → Lo compro. The pronouns lo, la, los, las agree with the grammatical gender and number of the object: las entradas → las. Me, te, nos and os can also be direct objects: ¿Me escuchas? Personal a may introduce a human direct object: Veo a Ana → La veo. It does not automatically require le. Keep track of the noun before replacing it. If two possible referents compete, repeat the noun instead of making the listener guess.

lectures.title: Position and interpretation
lectures.body: Place the pronoun before a conjugated verb: No la necesito. With an appropriate verb-plus-infinitive construction, either before the first verb or attached to the infinitive works: Lo quiero comprar / Quiero comprarlo. Never insert it between the preposition and infinitive in voy a comprarlo. Attached pronouns are one written word. Do not replace an entire sentence with a gendered noun pronoun without considering meaning; neutral lo can refer to an idea, as in no lo sé, a use you will develop later. Some regions use le for certain male human direct objects; recognize this documented variation while practicing the course’s lo/la system.

lectures.title: Keep the referent clear
lectures.body:
Suppose a shop assistant asks **¿Necesita la bolsa?** A useful answer is **Sí, la necesito**, because **la** retrieves the already identified bag. Without that shared context, **La necesito** leaves the listener wondering what you need. Pronouns reduce repetition only after the reference is sufficiently clear. In a longer exchange, repeat a noun when the topic changes: **La bolsa está bien, pero necesito las entradas. ¿Las tiene?**

The direct object can be a person. **Veo a Ana → La veo** shows why the personal **a** does not automatically create an indirect object. Ask what role the person plays in the event, rather than classifying every phrase beginning with **a** identically. Some regions use **le** for a male human direct object in accepted contexts; recognize this variation while practicing the broadly Latin American **lo/la** distinction here.

With two verbs, compare **Lo quiero comprar** and **Quiero comprarlo**. With a single ordinary finite verb, use **Lo compro**, not *comprolo*. Before substituting a pronoun, identify its referent, gender and number, and then choose a permitted position.

reading:
—¿Tienes las entradas para el concierto?
—Sí, las tengo en el teléfono.
—Perfecto. ¿Necesitamos imprimirlas?
—No, podemos mostrarlas en la puerta.
—¿Y el mapa? No lo encuentro.
—Lo voy a enviar ahora.
—Gracias. Veo a Ana en la estación. ¿La esperamos aquí?
—Sí, pero explica dónde estamos: hay dos puertas.
Encuentra el referente de las, lo y la. Después vuelve a contar la situación usando los sustantivos completos. Observa cuándo esa repetición ayuda y cuándo resulta innecesaria.

quiz.prompt: Choose the expression that communicates this meaning: I buy it (masculine).
quiz.explanation: “Lo compro” expresses “I buy it (masculine)”. “Podemos mostrarlas” instead means “We can show them (feminine)”. “¿Dónde las pongo?” instead means “Where do I put them (feminine)?”.

quiz.prompt: Choose the expression that communicates this meaning: I need it (feminine).
quiz.explanation: “La necesito” expresses “I need it (feminine)”. “Necesito el mapa” instead means “I need the map”. “No lo encuentro” instead means “I cannot find it”.

quiz.prompt: Choose the expression that communicates this meaning: I have them (feminine).
quiz.explanation: “Las tengo” expresses “I have them (feminine)”. “La esperamos aquí” instead means “We wait for her here”. “Prefiero repetir el nombre” instead means “I prefer to repeat the name”.

quiz.prompt: Choose the expression that communicates this meaning: I see them (masculine).
quiz.explanation: “Los veo” expresses “I see them (masculine)”. “Voy a enviarlo” instead means “I am going to send it”. “Lo compro” instead means “I buy it (masculine)”.

quiz.prompt: Choose the expression that communicates this meaning: I want to buy it.
quiz.explanation: “Quiero comprarlo” expresses “I want to buy it”. “La necesito” instead means “I need it (feminine)”. “¿Dónde las pongo?” instead means “Where do I put them (feminine)?”.

quiz.prompt: Match each English meaning to its Spanish expression. Use each expression once.
quiz.explanation: “Quiero comprarlo” means “I want to buy it”. “No la necesito” means “I do not need it (feminine)”. “Podemos mostrarlas” means “We can show them (feminine)”. Each alternative belongs to a different meaning; check the whole phrase, including its grammatical person and register.

This is the source model, not a text to submit unchanged. A successful adaptation retains the communicative purpose while changing relevant forms and facts. Compare with the worked examples for the reasons behind form choices.
homework.rubric: 0–3 each: fulfills the specified purpose; organized and comprehensible; target forms support meaning; revisions are explained with examples. 0 = no evidence, 1 = substantial help needed, 2 = effective with some support, 3 = independently effective for this task. Record who evaluated the work.

homework.prompt: Complete the resource assignment, or ask a willing reader to read the original text without showing it to you. First listen for the situation and purpose; listen again for three details and one contrast. Write a 60–100-word listening log naming the source, words actually heard, one uncertainty, and how you checked it. If using local synthesized speech, label it synthetic. Text-only preparation is not completed listening.
homework.model: A useful log separates the speaker’s message from your interpretation: “I heard [specific phrase]; I understood [claim]; I was uncertain about [word/relationship]; checking [text or partner] changed my interpretation to [correction].” Use the unit reading as an answer reference for a read-aloud version, never as evidence of an external speaker’s words.
homework.rubric: 0–2 each: identifies source and listening conditions; retrieves central meaning; supports three details; checks a specific uncertainty. Do not count a copied transcript as independent comprehension.

homework.prompt: Arrange tickets, a map and a meeting place. Use object pronouns, then deliberately ask which object your partner means when a reference is ambiguous.
homework.model: Use the original reading/dialogue and the sentence-pattern cards as preparation. Make a brief outline, then put it away. Your partner should introduce a detail you did not prepare. Respond, request clarification if needed, and summarize what you agreed or still disagree about. Solo fallback: record two possible viewpoints and improvise a response after a pause; label it rehearsal.
homework.rubric: 0–3 each: task fulfillment, comprehensibility, control of target language, responsiveness to another speaker. A partner or instructor should cite one example per score. Solo rehearsal provides no evidence for live responsiveness; mark that dimension not observed.

homework.prompt: On a later day, retrieve six cards without looking. Use three in a fresh response to the practical task. Identify one recurring form error and one communication difficulty. Produce a corrected example, explain the reason, and schedule a specific follow-up exchange or listening session.
homework.model: Compare your response with these two models: Lo compro / La necesito. A useful reflection explains the function, not just the spelling. Revisit the first worked item and create a different example of its principle.
homework.rubric: Report recall count separately from performance. Reflection is complete when it contains an observed difficulty, an explained correction, a fresh example, and an actionable next session.

task: Arrange tickets, a map and a meeting place. Use object pronouns, then deliberately ask which object your partner means when a reference is ambiguous.
culture: Leísmo varies by place and referent; some uses are accepted in standard descriptions, especially masculine singular persons. Recognition of variation does not mean every pronoun is interchangeable in every context.
selfAssessment: I can identify direct objects in familiar sentences.
I can choose and place lo, la, los and las.
I can clarify a pronoun’s referent in a transaction.
remediation: Sort mistakes by form, meaning, and interaction. For form errors, explain a worked example and create a contrasting pair. For comprehension errors, replay a short segment or use a willing reader and verify your interpretation. For interaction difficulties, repeat the practical task with one new constraint. Compare evidence across days; repeated selection of a known answer alone is not mastery.
